screens.title: Password Management and Security Policies
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to make passwords a reliable defense, not a weak link. We focus on MySQL's built-in enforcement through the validate_password plugin, how to apply policy levels and tune variables, and how to manage the lifecycle of accounts through expiration and locking. You will also learn why MySQL stores only hashes and what that means for recovery and breach resistance. We'll ground the concepts in short operational examples: checking plugin settings, changing the global policy, creating a user with a compliant password, setting password expiration, and locking an account during an incident. I will also highlight common mistakes DBAs make, like leaving default policies in place or using non-rotated service passwords, and practical mitigations such as programmatic rotation and audit checks. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to configure a strong policy, enforce regular rotation, respond quickly to suspicious activity, and explain why these steps reduce risk. Think about the last time a user reported suspicious access; locking the account and forcing a password change is often the fastest containment step.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Password Management and Security Policies
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson: practical configuration and incident response

Password Management and Security Policies

Understand how MySQL enforces complexity, how to rotate and expire credentials, and how to react when an account is suspected of compromise.

Validate Plugin
Enforces password complexity rules and prevents weak credentials.
Lifecycle
Expiration and locking let you force rotation and contain compromises quickly.
Storage
MySQL stores password hashes not plain text, reducing damage if tables are read.
Operational
Auditing, rotation, and external two-factor add practical defense layers.
Visual concept
Policy
LOW, MEDIUM, STRONG — controls checks and dictionary use.
Lifecycle
Expire, force change, lock accounts during incidents.
Storage
One-way hashes protect credentials in the user table.
Explore Key Topics
validate_password
Configures complexity and blocks weak passwords at creation and change time.
Expiration & Lock
Force rotation and rapidly cut access during incidents by expiring or locking accounts.
Storage & Hashing
MySQL uses secure hashing by default; never store plain text passwords.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives are practical and measurable. First, you will configure and enforce strong password policies using MySQL's validate_password plugin, including policy levels and the key variables that control length, digit and special character counts. Second, you'll manage account lifecycle attributes such as forcing password expiration, setting intervals, and locking or unlocking accounts as an immediate containment step. Third, you will understand how MySQL stores credentials securely by hashing with modern algorithms and why plain text or weak hashes are unacceptable. Fourth, you will adopt operational best practices: schedule rotation for human and service accounts, audit password changes, and avoid common pitfalls like default passwords. Each objective links a configuration task to a practical outcome. For example, setting a STRONG policy and a sensible minimum length prevents weak credentials from being set in the first place. Understanding expiration and locking lets you respond quickly when compromise is suspected. These skills are essential for any DBA responsible for reducing the attack surface of a production database.

screens.title: Why password management matters
screens.narratorSegment: Effective password management is the foundation of access control for a database server. A weak or reused password is often the easiest path for an attacker to gain persistent access. When you enforce policy at the server level, you reduce the number of accounts that can be exploited. In MySQL, the validate_password plugin provides a single, consistent place to check strength rules whenever a password is created or changed. Beyond blocking short or simple passwords, lifecycle controls such as expiration and locking give you a playbook to limit exposure: expiration forces rotation so a leaked password has a limited window of usefulness, while locking an account immediately stops active misuse without deleting the user. A concrete example: if an application credential is suspected of being exposed, locking the account and expiring the password prevents further use until you investigate and rotate credentials. A common misconception is that longer intervals and no expiration are acceptable for convenience; in practice that choice lengthens the window of vulnerability. Key takeaway: combine preventive rules with lifecycle and response actions so passwords become an active part of your defense.

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: Policy enforcement plus lifecycle controls reduce successful compromise and limit blast radius when credentials are exposed.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Why password management matters
Definition

Passwords as risk controls

Passwords limit who can authenticate. Enforcing complexity and rotation makes guessing and credential reuse harder, and locking provides immediate containment when you suspect an account is compromised.

Concrete example
If a developer reports odd behavior, lock the user account and force password expiry. This stops access and requires a new password before use resumes.
Common mistake
Relying on default or weak policy levels because they are easier to manage increases exposure across all users.
Key takeaway
Treat password policy and lifecycle as active security controls, not administrative chores.
Operational scenario
Scenario: suspected credential leak
-- immediate steps
ALTER USER 'suspicious_user'@'%' ACCOUNT LOCK;
ALTER USER 'suspicious_user'@'%' PASSWORD EXPIRE;
-- follow up: rotate credentials and audit access logs

screens.title: validate_password plugin and policy levels
screens.narratorSegment: The validate_password plugin enforces complexity rules whenever a password is created or changed. It exposes a policy level that you can set to LOW, MEDIUM, or STRONG. LOW performs a basic minimum-length check. MEDIUM adds checks for digit counts, mixed case, and special characters. STRONG includes a dictionary check to prevent common words. For production databases, STRONG is recommended because it not only requires mixed character types and length but also rejects passwords found in a dictionary, which stops many predictable passwords. A clear example: a password that meets MEDIUM might include numbers and punctuation but still be a common phrase; STRONG would reject that if it appears in the dictionary. A common misconception is assuming MEDIUM is 'good enough' for all environments. In high-value systems, the additional dictionary check in STRONG materially reduces risk. When you set policy to STRONG and tune minimum length and character counts, you create a predictable barrier that prevents many successful guessing attacks and password spraying attempts. validate_password plugin and policy levels means low checks length, medium adds character classes, strong adds a dictionary check — strong is preferred for production.. In practical terms, how low, medium, and strong differ and why strong is recommended. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › validate_password plugin and policy levels
Policy level comparison
LOW
Minimum length checks only. Useful for non-production or development but risky in public environments.
MEDIUM
Enforces numbers, mixed case, and special characters. Good baseline for many teams.
STRONG
Includes dictionary checks to stop common words. Recommended for production systems.
Key Takeaway

Choose STRONG for production and tune length and counts to match your threat model.

Tuneable variables
validate_password.policy  -- 0=LOW,1=MEDIUM,2=STRONG
validate_password.length
validate_password.number_count
validate_password.special_char_count
validate_password.mixed_case_count
Example
Set policy to STRONG and minimum length to 12 or more for higher assurance.

screens.title: Inspect and change validate_password settings
screens.narratorSegment: Start by checking whether validate_password is active and what settings are applied. Use the system variables listing for validate_password to inspect policy, length, and character counts. If the plugin is missing, you can install it, but always verify the current runtime behavior before changing anything. To make a runtime change, set the GLOBAL variables for policy and length. This affects new password checks immediately but will not persist across restarts unless you add equivalent lines to the server configuration file. A concrete example: set the policy to STRONG and minimum length to fourteen. After changing runtime variables, flush privileges or restart to ensure the persistence is tested if you also updated my. cnf. A common misconception is that a runtime set is persistent; remind yourself that only configuration file edits survive a restart. Practice verifying the effective settings after each change to confirm enforcement is active. Inspect and change validate_password settings means set global changes take effect immediately but must be mirrored in my.cnf to persist through a restart.. In practical terms, show variables, set policy and length at runtime, and persist changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Runtime vs persistent
keyIdea.text: SET GLOBAL changes take effect immediately but must be mirrored in my.cnf to persist through a restart.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Inspect and change validate_password settings
Common commands
Check current variables
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'validate_password%';
Set strong policy and length at runtime
SET GLOBAL validate_password.policy = 2; -- STRONG
SET GLOBAL validate_password.length = 14;
Remember to persist in my.cnf
# my.cnf
validate_password.policy=2
validate_password.length=14
Explanation and example
  • SHOW VARIABLES reveals the active settings so you can confirm enforcement before creating users.
  • SET GLOBAL changes are immediate for new password checks but are lost on restart unless persisted.
  • Update my.cnf and restart to maintain a consistent configuration across restarts.
  • After applying, attempt to create a user with a weak password as a test to confirm behavior.
Takeaway

Always verify active settings and persist changes to avoid configuration drift.

screens.title: Demonstrate password rejection and creation
screens.narratorSegment: A hands-on test helps you confirm that your policy actually blocks weak credentials. First, try to create a user with a short or simple password. MySQL will return an error explaining which policy rule failed, guiding the user to choose a stronger password. Then craft a password that satisfies minimum length, digit and special character counts, and mixed case — or use a generated password from your vault — and create the user successfully. The important lesson is not the exact text of the error but the operational feedback loop: enforcement informs the user, and the system prevents a weak secret from being stored. A common inexperienced approach is to ignore the error and lower the policy; instead, educate users and provide approved ways to generate compliant passwords. After creating a compliant account, verify the user exists and that the authentication method and host restrictions are correct. This approach turns policy into reproducible behavior rather than an aspirational guideline. Demonstrate password rejection and creation means try a weak password to see the rejection, then create a compliant user to confirm the policy is effective.. In practical terms, try a weak password, observe error, then create a compliant user. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Demonstrate password rejection and creation
Terminal: weak password attempt
Attempt create with an intentionally weak password
CREATE USER 'dev_test_user'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'short';
-- Expected: error rejecting due to policy
Observe the rejection message. Learn which variable caused the failure and adjust the password rather than lowering policy in production.
Terminal: compliant creation
Create user with a compliant password
CREATE USER 'dev_test_user'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'DevTestSecurePass!14';
-- Expected: user created successfully
Verification
Query mysql.user or use SHOW GRANTS to confirm the account and its host restrictions.
Pro tip
Use a secrets manager to generate and store complex service passwords instead of embedding them in scripts.

screens.title: Password expiration and rotation
screens.narratorSegment: Password expiration enforces periodic rotation so credentials do not remain valid forever. MySQL offers two main ways to expire a password: set an interval so it expires after a number of days, or expire immediately so the user must change at next login. For example, applying a 90 day interval forces users to change their password on a fixed cadence. Expire immediately when you suspect compromise so the next successful login must change the password before any other commands are allowed. For service accounts you might choose never to expire, but that comes with responsibility: restrict privileges and automate rotation through your deployment pipeline. A common pitfall is setting very long intervals for convenience, which increases exposure. Another is assuming expiration alone prevents abuse; combine it with audits and programmatic rotation for service accounts. A practical exercise is to set a 30 day expiry for a test user and then connect as that user after expiry to observe the forced change workflow. Password expiration and rotation means use expiration intervals for regular rotation and immediate expiry during incidents; avoid overly long intervals.. In practical terms, use expiry intervals and immediate expiry to enforce rotation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use expiration intervals for regular rotation and immediate expiry during incidents; avoid overly long intervals.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Password expiration and rotation
Expiration examples
ALTER USER 'app_user'@'localhost' PASSWORD EXPIRE INTERVAL 90 DAY; -- expires after 90 days
ALTER USER 'admin_user'@'localhost' PASSWORD EXPIRE; -- expires immediately at next login
ALTER USER 'service_account'@'%' PASSWORD EXPIRE NEVER; -- no expiration (use with caution)
Example
Set dev users to 30 days to encourage frequent rotation during development cycles.
Common mistake
Applying NEVER for many accounts for convenience increases long-term risk.
Takeaway

Use expiry intervals for human accounts and reserve non-expiring passwords for tightly controlled service accounts with programmatic rotation and strict privilege limits.

Check your understanding

When would you choose immediate expiry over an interval, and how would you test the result?

screens.title: Locking and unlocking accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Account locking is an important immediate containment tool. When you suspect an account is compromised, locking prevents further connections instantly while preserving the user record for investigation. Use the account lock command to disable authentication attempts without dropping the user. Later, after investigation and any required rotation, unlock the account. A concrete workflow: lock the account as soon as suspicious activity is detected, run an audit to gather evidence, expire the password to force a reset, then unlock once the new credentials are in place. A common misconception is that revoking privileges is sufficient; a connection may still succeed depending on credential and connection state. Locking is explicit and immediate. Practice by locking a test user, attempting a client connection to see the failure, then unlocking and confirming normal access after a password change. This creates a repeatable incident containment playbook. Locking and unlocking accounts means account lock immediately blocks access while preserving the user for investigation and recovery.. In practical terms, use account lock as immediate containment during incidents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Locking and unlocking accounts
Locking commands
-- Lock an account
ALTER USER 'compromised_user'@'localhost' ACCOUNT LOCK;
-- Unlock an account
ALTER USER 'compromised_user'@'localhost' ACCOUNT UNLOCK;
Locking is immediate and prevents connections. Keep the user record to retain grants and metadata for investigation.
Incident playbook
  1. Lock the suspected account to stop access immediately.
  2. Audit recent connections and queries for evidence of misuse.
  3. Expire the password to require a reset before reactivation.
  4. Unlock after rotation and verification.
Example test
Lock a test account, attempt a client connection to confirm rejection, then unlock and test again after reset.

screens.title: Secure password storage and hashing
screens.narratorSegment: MySQL never stores plaintext passwords; instead it stores one-way cryptographic hashes so that an attacker who reads the user table cannot retrieve usable credentials directly. MySQL 8.0 uses modern routines and caching mechanisms by default to protect authentication data. The practical effect is that a database leak yields hashes, not passwords, which raises the attacker's work factor substantially. However, hashing is only one part of the defense: use strong algorithms, keep software patched, and protect access to the user table itself. A common misconception is that hashing alone solves all credential problems. In reality, attackers can perform offline cracking attempts if hashes are exposed, so combine hashing with policy enforcement, rotation, and monitoring. For high-sensitivity administrative access, require additional controls such as two-factor authentication implemented outside MySQL, for example at an SSH gateway or proxy. The takeaway: secure hashing reduces risk but must be combined with operational controls to be effective. Secure password storage and hashing means hashes are irreversible representations; combine strong hashing with rotation and monitoring to limit offline cracking risk.. In practical terms, why mysql stores hashes and the role of strong algorithms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Secure password storage and hashing
Concept

MySQL stores a one-way hash of the password. On login, the supplied password is hashed and compared to the stored value. Matching hashes mean authentication succeeds without ever storing the plain password.

Practical note
Do not attempt to store readable passwords or implement custom weak hashing. Rely on MySQL's secure defaults and keep the server patched.
Operational controls
  • Treat the mysql.user table as sensitive; limit access to it.
  • Combine hashed storage with policy enforcement to reduce the chance of successful offline attacks.
  • Rotate high-privilege credentials regularly and monitor for suspicious password change attempts.
Key takeaway

Hashing protects stored credentials but must be part of a layered approach including policy, rotation, and monitoring.

screens.title: Service accounts vs human accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Service accounts and human accounts have different operational needs and risk profiles. Human accounts should expire regularly and require interactive resets because humans can change passwords and are subject to policy-driven workflows. Service accounts often need non-expiring credentials for automation, but leaving them unrotated is risky. Best practice is to minimize privileges for service accounts, restrict host bindings, and rotate their secrets programmatically on a strict schedule using your deployment or secret manager. A concrete example: allowing PASSWORD EXPIRE NEVER for a service account can be acceptable if the account has a narrow scope, is rotated by automation every thirty days, and its credentials are stored securely. A common misunderstanding is to apply the same expiration cadence to service accounts without automation; that breaks automation and often leads teams to disable expiry entirely. The pragmatic approach balances operational continuity with security controls such as limited grants, network restrictions, and automated rotation. Service accounts vs human accounts means human accounts: frequent expiry and interactive resets. service accounts: restricted privileges and automated rotation when using non-expiring credentials.. In practical terms, why treatment and rotation differ for service credentials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Human accounts
Expire regularly, require interactive password changes, and educate users about generation of unique, strong passwords. Enforce STRONG policy for interactive users where possible.
Example
Set a 60 to 90 day expiry for human users to reduce exposure while balancing workload.
Service accounts
Consider PASSWORD EXPIRE NEVER only when you implement automated rotation, restrict privileges, and monitor access closely.
Best practice

screens.title: Audit, monitoring, and two-factor considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Audit and monitoring complement password policies. Track password change attempts and failed authentication events because a spike in failures often precedes a successful compromise. Use MySQL's auditing or general query log to collect evidence of problematic activity and alert on repeated failures. For administrative access, consider implementing two-factor authentication outside of MySQL, such as at an SSH jump host or an authentication proxy that enforces TFA before forwarding connections. This is important because MySQL itself does not provide native two-factor for client logins. A practical scenario: if you see multiple failed login attempts followed by a password change event, treat this as suspicious and apply the containment workflow: lock the account, expire the password, and investigate connected hosts. Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Audit, monitoring, and two-factor considerations
Monitoring checklist
  • Log password changes and failed authentication attempts.
  • Create alerts for spikes in failed logins or unexpected password resets.
  • Retain logs long enough to support incident investigation and correlation.
Two-factor options
Enforce TFA outside MySQL: SSH jump hosts, proxies, or an LDAP gateway that requires TFA before allowing database connections.
Incident scenario
If you detect failed logins followed by a password change, lock the user, expire the password, and gather logs from the client and server for correlation before unlocking.
Why this matters

Detection plus containment reduces attacker dwell time and prevents misuse of rotated credentials.

screens.title: Hands-on scenario: enforce strong policy and lock a test account

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Hands-on scenario
Step-by-step
  1. Install or verify validate_password plugin is active.
  2. SET GLOBAL validate_password.policy = 2 and set a minimum length of 14.
  3. Create the test user with a compliant password to confirm creation succeeds.
  4. ALTER USER ... PASSWORD EXPIRE INTERVAL 30 DAY to set lifecycle policy.
  5. ALTER USER ... ACCOUNT LOCK to simulate an incident, then test client connection to confirm blocking.
Verification
Run SHOW VARIABLES and attempt a weak CREATE to confirm rejection, then verify the locked account cannot connect.
Analogy
Think of the policy as a gate that only allows sufficiently strong keys, expiry as scheduled key replacement, and locking as turning the lock to block entry during a breach.
Practice prompt

Try this in a sandbox and write down the observed rejection message when a weak password is used.

In this chapter you will learn how to make passwords a reliable defense, not a weak link. We focus on MySQL's built-in enforcement through the validate_password plugin, how to apply policy levels and tune variables, and how to manage the lifecycle of accounts through expiration and locking. You will also learn why MySQL stores only hashes and what that means for recovery and breach resistance. We'll ground the concepts in short operational examples: checking plugin settings, changing the global policy, creating a user with a compliant password, setting password expiration, and locking an account during an incident. I will also highlight common mistakes DBAs make, like leaving default policies in place or using non-rotated service passwords, and practical mitigations such as programmatic rotation and audit checks. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to configure a strong policy, enforce regular rotation, respond quickly to suspicious activity, and explain why these steps reduce risk. Think about the last time a user reported suspicious access; locking the account and forcing a password change is often the fastest containment step.

These learning objectives are practical and measurable. First, you will configure and enforce strong password policies using MySQL's validate_password plugin, including policy levels and the key variables that control length, digit and special character counts. Second, you'll manage account lifecycle attributes such as forcing password expiration, setting intervals, and locking or unlocking accounts as an immediate containment step. Third, you will understand how MySQL stores credentials securely by hashing with modern algorithms and why plain text or weak hashes are unacceptable. Fourth, you will adopt operational best practices: schedule rotation for human and service accounts, audit password changes, and avoid common pitfalls like default passwords. Each objective links a configuration task to a practical outcome. For example, setting a STRONG policy and a sensible minimum length prevents weak credentials from being set in the first place. Understanding expiration and locking lets you respond quickly when compromise is suspected. These skills are essential for any DBA responsible for reducing the attack surface of a production database.

This second objectives slide expands the hands-on skills you will practice. You will verify whether the validate_password plugin is active and inspect its runtime variables, which matters because you must confirm enforcement is actually applied. You will practice setting global variables at runtime and making persistent changes in the server configuration so policies survive restarts. You will simulate a weak password creation to observe MySQL's rejection and then create a compliant user, reinforcing the practical effect of enforcement. You will perform account locking and unlocking to see how immediate containment works, and then test a locked account to observe the login error. Each of these tasks translates policy into predictable operational controls. Knowing how to check, change, and test configuration gives you confidence that policies are working and provides a repeatable playbook during an incident.

Effective password management is the foundation of access control for a database server. A weak or reused password is often the easiest path for an attacker to gain persistent access. When you enforce policy at the server level, you reduce the number of accounts that can be exploited. In MySQL, the validate_password plugin provides a single, consistent place to check strength rules whenever a password is created or changed. Beyond blocking short or simple passwords, lifecycle controls such as expiration and locking give you a playbook to limit exposure: expiration forces rotation so a leaked password has a limited window of usefulness, while locking an account immediately stops active misuse without deleting the user. A concrete example: if an application credential is suspected of being exposed, locking the account and expiring the password prevents further use until you investigate and rotate credentials. A common misconception is that longer intervals and no expiration are acceptable for convenience; in practice that choice lengthens the window of vulnerability. Key takeaway: combine preventive rules with lifecycle and response actions so passwords become an active part of your defense.

The validate_password plugin enforces complexity rules whenever a password is created or changed. It exposes a policy level that you can set to LOW, MEDIUM, or STRONG. LOW performs a basic minimum-length check. MEDIUM adds checks for digit counts, mixed case, and special characters. STRONG includes a dictionary check to prevent common words. For production databases, STRONG is recommended because it not only requires mixed character types and length but also rejects passwords found in a dictionary, which stops many predictable passwords. A clear example: a password that meets MEDIUM might include numbers and punctuation but still be a common phrase; STRONG would reject that if it appears in the dictionary. A common misconception is assuming MEDIUM is 'good enough' for all environments. In high-value systems, the additional dictionary check in STRONG materially reduces risk. When you set policy to STRONG and tune minimum length and character counts, you create a predictable barrier that prevents many successful guessing attacks and password spraying attempts. validate_password plugin and policy levels means low checks length, medium adds character classes, strong adds a dictionary check — strong is preferred for production.. In practical terms, how low, medium, and strong differ and why strong is recommended. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
